text: The Azure SDK for Python and Boto3 aren't one SDK each — the Azure SDK is actually dozens of small packages, one per service area, while AWS's Boto3 is a single package covering nearly every service. Both reduce to the same shape once you're past the import line.

Azure splits its SDK into azure-mgmt packages — azure-mgmt-compute for virtual machines, azure-mgmt-storage for storage accounts, azure-mgmt-network for networking, azure-mgmt-resource for resource groups, with azure-identity handling authentication separately, covered next lesson. Every single one of them follows the exact same shape: build a client object from a credential and a subscription ID, then call methods on it.

Once that client exists, using it reads almost like plain English. compute_client.virtual_machines.list_all() returns real virtual machine objects, not raw JSON you'd have to parse by hand — each one with a usable dot-name, dot-location, and every other property the Azure REST API exposes, already converted into a proper Python object.

Boto3 takes a different shape: one package, boto3, covering almost every AWS service, with two ways in. boto3 dot client gives you the low-level interface, mirroring the AWS API call for call — describe_instances, create_bucket, exactly as AWS names them. boto3 dot resource is the higher-level, more Pythonic layer, available for a subset of services like S3, letting you write s3.buckets.all() instead of parsing a raw response dictionary.

Strip away the package names and both SDKs do the same three things: import the package, build a client — or a resource — using real credentials, then call a method and get structured data back. Azure hands you typed objects; Boto3's client calls hand you nested dictionaries shaped like the AWS API's own JSON.

Both SDKs need one more piece before any of this runs: real credentials. Lesson 11 covers exactly how DefaultAzureCredential and Boto3's credential chain each find those credentials — and why hardcoding a key or secret directly in the script is the one approach both of them are built to avoid.
